title: Java Concurrency Revision Notes
summary: Quick night-before revision of Java concurrency: threads, executors, synchronization and visibility, locks and atomics, concurrent collections, CompletableFuture, and the pitfalls that cause bugs in production.

chapters.title: Threads and Runnable Mental Model
points: A thread is an independent path of execution sharing the process heap; each thread has its own stack and program counter
Runnable describes the task (void run()); Callable<V> returns a value and may throw a checked exception; Thread is the worker that runs it
start() creates a new thread and calls run() on it; calling run() directly just executes on the current thread
Thread states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED
Interview Point: Runnable vs Callable? start() vs run()? Why prefer implementing Runnable over extending Thread? What does join() do?

chapters.title: ExecutorService and Thread Pools
points: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread management: submit(task) returns a Future, execute(task) returns nothing
Factories: newFixedThreadPool(n), newCachedThreadPool() (unbounded threads), newSingleThreadExecutor(), newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() (Java 21)
Future.get() blocks until the result is ready and wraps task exceptions in ExecutionException; get(timeout, unit) throws TimeoutException
Shutdown correctly: shutdown() stops accepting tasks and lets queued ones finish; shutdownNow() interrupts workers; follow with awaitTermination()
ThreadPoolExecutor params: corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, workQueue, RejectedExecutionHandler; extra threads above core are only created once the queue is full

Interview Point: How does ThreadPoolExecutor decide when to add threads? Why avoid Executors.newFixedThreadPool with its unbounded queue in production? submit vs execute exception handling? Fixed vs cached pool?

chapters.title: synchronized and volatile
points: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility: one thread at a time holds the object's monitor, and releasing it publishes writes to the next acquirer
Instance synchronized method locks this; static synchronized locks the Class object; a synchronized block locks any object you choose, so prefer a private final lock
volatile guarantees visibility and ordering (happens-before) for a variable but NOT atomicity: volatile int count; count++ is still a race
Use volatile for a simple stop flag or safely published immutable reference; use synchronized when a check-then-act or compound update is involved
wait()/notify()/notifyAll() must be called while holding the monitor, and wait must sit in a while loop to guard against spurious wakeups
Interview Point: What is happens-before? Why is count++ on a volatile not thread-safe? Which object does a static synchronized method lock? Why wait in a while loop, not an if?

chapters.title: Locks and Atomic Classes
points: ReentrantLock gives explicit lock()/unlock(); always unlock in finally, and the same thread may re-acquire it (reentrant)
ReentrantLock extras over synchronized: tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly(), fairness option, multiple Conditions
ReadWriteLock (ReentrantReadWriteLock) allows many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer; good for read-heavy data
AtomicInteger/AtomicLong use CAS (compare-and-set) for lock-free updates: incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet(expected, new), updateAndGet(fn)
LongAdder beats AtomicLong under heavy contention for counters, but sum() is not an atomic snapshot

Interview Point: synchronized vs ReentrantLock? How does CAS work and what is the ABA problem? When choose LongAdder over AtomicLong? What causes deadlock and how do you prevent it with lock ordering?

chapters.title: ConcurrentHashMap and CompletableFuture
points: ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and fine-grained locked writes (per bin, CAS on empty bins); it does not allow null keys or values
Use atomic methods, not check-then-put: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge(key, 1, Integer::sum); get-then-put on separate calls is a race
Compared with Collections.synchronizedMap (one lock for every call) and Hashtable, ConcurrentHashMap scales; its iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException
CompletableFuture chain: supplyAsync(() -> x).thenApply(f).thenCompose(g).thenCombine(other, fn).exceptionally(ex -> default)
Without an explicit executor, async stages run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool; pass your own executor for blocking IO work, and use allOf/anyOf to join several futures
Interview Point: Why does ConcurrentHashMap reject null? thenApply vs thenCompose? How do you handle exceptions in a CompletableFuture chain? Why is computeIfAbsent safer than get then put?

chapters.title: Concurrency Pitfalls and Cheat Sheet
points: Race condition: unsynchronized check-then-act or read-modify-write; fix with atomics, locks or concurrent collections
Deadlock needs circular lock waiting; prevent by acquiring locks in a fixed global order or using tryLock with timeout
Never swallow InterruptedException: restore with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or rethrow
Prefer immutability and thread confinement; use ThreadLocal sparingly and remove() in pooled threads to avoid leaks
Cheat sheet: stop flag → volatile; compound update → synchronized/atomic; counter → AtomicInteger/LongAdder; shared map → ConcurrentHashMap; async pipeline → CompletableFuture with own executor
Interview Point: What are the four conditions for deadlock? How do you handle InterruptedException properly? What is the difference between a race condition and a data race?
